idiom_name: DRb: DRbObject proxy (forwarder) + DRb.start_service front object (receiver), Marshal payloads
implementation_notes: DRb is the pattern as a library: DRb.start_service('druby://host:port', front_object) publishes a peer object and runs the receiver - Marshal-decoded calls dispatched by method name to the front object - while DRbObject.new_with_uri('druby://peer2:9002') gives the caller a proxy that marshals method calls and results, so the classic Forwarder and Receiver classes are not written at all and only the front object (the peer) belongs to the application. Since Ruby 3.4 drb is a bundled gem rather than a default gem, so it must be listed in the Gemfile. Where the peer is not Ruby or the wire format must be fixed, drop to a Socket plus length-prefixed Marshal.dump/JSON loop, which puts both roles back into your code.
code_sketch:
require 'drb/drb'

class Ledger                                # the peer (server side)
  def reserve(id, qty) = id + qty           # invoked remotely
end

DRb.start_service('druby://0.0.0.0:9002', Ledger.new)   # receiver + dispatch
DRb.thread.join

# forwarder: the proxy marshals the call and the result
ledger = DRbObject.new_with_uri('druby://peer2:9002')
ref = ledger.reserve(7, 3)
pitfalls: Marshal.load on data from an untrusted peer is code execution, and DRb has no authentication by default - bind to a trusted network or tunnel it (TLS/SSH).
DRb.start_service must run in every process, including forked children, or callbacks fail with a connection error.
The proxy raises DRb::DRbConnError only when the call is made, so an unreachable peer looks like a delayed exception rather than a startup failure.
